profiles.name: Norma Lugo Maldonado
profiles.description: Norma Lugo Maldonado was arrested during the 2000 civil-disobedience campaign against U.S. Navy training on Vieques, Puerto Rico. The First Circuit identifies this person among defendants arrested between April and June 2000 after entering Camp García to oppose the exercises and their effects on residents and the environment. Following a nonjury trial, the defendant was convicted under 18 U.S.C. § 1382. The consolidated appeal, United States v. Sued-Jiménez, upheld the convictions on December 19, 2001. The opinion does not specify this defendant’s sentence or the length of physical confinement.
profiles.finding: Puerto Rico Senate record is a documentary lead. Genealogy Norma Lugo 1920–2010 is not independently matched; no verified portrait.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public availability does not establish permission.

profiles.name: Sergei Chaparin
profiles.description: Sergei Chaparin was a Russian-born U.S. Army cook assigned to the 1st Infantry Division in Vilseck, Germany. He served from June 2001 until November 2004 and pursued a conscientious-objector application for nine months. The chaplain, psychologist, investigating officer and his commander recommended approval, and Army headquarters granted an honorable discharge. No arrest or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Photographer Sergei Chaparin websites found, but no independent link to the Russian-born Vilseck Army cook. Hold as unverified namesake.

profiles.name: Travis Clark
profiles.description: Travis Clark was a Marine reservist from Plantation, Florida who joined at age 19 in 1996. In March 2003, with about a year remaining on his contract, he publicly said he would refuse deployment to Iraq because he opposed the invasion. The available contemporaneous report describes a conditional refusal; it does not establish that his unit called him, that he disobeyed an order, or that he was arrested, court-martialed or confined.
profiles.finding: DVIDS casualty officer, contractor, airman and historical activist results are not matched to the Plantation Marine reservist.

profiles.name: David Cortelyou
profiles.description: David Cortelyou joined the U.S. Army in November 2004 and served in Iraq from January 14, 2006 to January 13, 2007 as a fire-support specialist, driver, machine gunner and radio operator. After returning to Germany and struggling with depression and suicidal thoughts, he went absent without leave twice rather than redeploy. He turned himself in after a 29-day absence and was separated from the Army in 2007. Available accounts do not document jail or stockade confinement.
profiles.finding: Connection e.V. Winter Soldier 2009 biography matches enlistment, deployment and AWOL history. Retain testifier biography PDF and event media for portrait verification; no captioned portrait verified.

profiles.name: Jeremy Daniel
profiles.description: Jeremy Daniel was a U.S. Army soldier at Fort Campbell who left for Canada with fellow soldier Bethany “Skyler” James in September 2007 rather than participate in the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. They drove to Cornwall, Ontario, where war-resister supporters helped them begin immigration proceedings. The accessible record documents his departure and refugee claim but no subsequent U.S. arrest, court-martial or confinement.
profiles.finding: Jeremy Daniel West, Smith, Burnham and Evans results are unrelated or unverified namesakes. Courage to Resist index remains a lead.

profiles.name: Michael Espinal
profiles.description: Michael Espinal was a U.S. Army Iraq veteran who went to Canada after refusing further participation in the war. By January 2008 he and his partner held Canadian work permits and lived in Sudbury, Ontario while pursuing immigration relief. Contemporary coverage described possible court-martial and imprisonment if he returned to the United States, but did not report that either had occurred. No exact birth date or later custody record was located.
profiles.finding: Sudbury.com war-resisters report matches context. Marine and Montana student portraits not independently matched. Follow up article imagery.

profiles.name: Dan Felushko
profiles.description: Dan Felushko was a Marine private first class and dual U.S.-Canadian citizen who left Camp Pendleton for Canada rather than deploy to Kuwait in January 2003 for the invasion of Iraq. He publicly explained that he saw no connection between the September 11 attacks and Iraq. He remained in Canada under his Canadian citizenship. Available reports document desertion allegations but no U.S. arrest, court-martial or confinement.

profiles.name: Brad Gaskins
profiles.description: Brad Gaskins was a U.S. Army sergeant who enlisted at 17 and served in Kosovo and on two combat tours in Iraq. After returning from Iraq in February 2006, he sought treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder and severe depression at Fort Drum. He left the post without leave in August 2006 when he believed he could not obtain adequate care. Civilian and military police arrested him on November 14, 2007 while his lawyer was arranging his surrender. He was transferred to Walter Reed Army Medical Center on November 16 for evaluation. The available reports do not document jail or stockade confinement, a court-martial, or the final disposition of the Army case.
profiles.finding: Veterans for Common Sense 2007 PTSD report and Workers World newspaper remain photo leads; image identity and credit unresolved.

profiles.name: Andrew Gorby
profiles.description: Andrew Gorby was a U.S. Army second lieutenant who became a conscientious objector while serving as an infantry officer. The Army discharged him as a conscientious objector in May 2007. He later worked with the Center on Conscience & War and joined public advocacy supporting service members who refused participation in war on grounds of conscience. His discharge was administrative; no arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.

profiles.name: Kevin Hicks
profiles.description: Kevin Hicks was a U.S. Army combat engineer with the 1st Armored Division who served in Iraq from September 2003 to August 2004. His experience there led him to oppose participation in all war, and he applied for conscientious-objector status with fellow soldier Vincent LaVolpa. After delays in the review process, the Army granted Hicks an honorable discharge in December 2005. He returned to Portland, Oregon and became involved in peace and counter-recruitment work. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.

profiles.name: Kyle Huwer
profiles.description: Kyle Huwer was a U.S. Army systems operator with the 22nd Signal Brigade who served from June 2004 to April 2006. With assistance from the Military Counseling Network in Germany, he applied for recognition as a conscientious objector after concluding that continued participation in war violated his beliefs. The Army granted him an honorable conscientious-objector discharge in April 2006. The proceeding involved no documented arrest, court-martial or confinement.

When ordered to Afghanistan while that application was pending, he publicly said he would not deploy. An October 2008 interview documented his opposition to war and his decision to resist; it did not establish the eventual disposition of his application or any criminal sentence.

profiles.name: Skyler James
profiles.description: Skyler James, born Bethany Smith, was a U.S. Army private at Fort Campbell who left for Canada with fellow soldier Jeremy Daniel in September 2007 rather than deploy to Afghanistan. She opposed the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and also described daily anti-LGBTQ harassment, threats and violence within her unit. Canada’s Federal Court ruled in November 2009 that the rejection of her refugee claim was unreasonable and ordered a new hearing; the refugee board later rejected the claim again. The available record does not document a U.S. arrest, court-martial or confinement.

profiles.name: Dale Landry
profiles.description: Dale Landry served in the U.S. Air Force on transport missions to Afghanistan. Facing an Iraq deployment that he opposed, he left for Canada rather than participate. Sources disagree on whether his departure occurred in 2004 or 2007, so no exact departure date is asserted. By 2012 he was living and working in Toronto while contesting removal from Canada. Reports described the risk of arrest if he returned to the United States, but do not document an actual U.S. arrest, court-martial or confinement.

profiles.name: Vincent LaVolpa
profiles.description: Vincent LaVolpa was a decorated U.S. Army combat engineer and Iraq veteran. At a checkpoint in Iraq he stopped himself from firing at an approaching family and shot out the vehicle’s tires instead, an experience that helped convince him he could no longer participate in war. He applied for conscientious-objector discharge alongside Kevin Hicks and received support from the Military Counseling Network. Contemporary accounts document delays in the administrative process but no arrest, court-martial or confinement, and the accessible reports do not establish the application’s final disposition.

profiles.name: Calvin Lee
profiles.description: Calvin Lee was a U.S. Army specialist and permanent resident from Southeast Asia assigned to the 58th Combat Engineer Company at Fort Irwin. A recruiter had told him that his work as a mechanic would not conflict with his Buddhist and Taoist beliefs. After the Army extended his September 2007 separation date under stop-loss and prepared to deploy his unit to Iraq, Lee applied for conscientious-objector status. His officers, chaplain and mental-health interviewer recommended approval, but the Army denied the application. On October 19, 2007, the ACLU filed a federal habeas action seeking his discharge. The accessible record does not establish the lawsuit’s final disposition and documents no arrest, court-martial or confinement.
profiles.finding: Malaysiakini identifies Calvin Lee Chee Keong, Buddhist 58th Combat Engineer CO. DVIDS healthcare specialist and historical military namesakes not matched.

profiles.name: Matthew Lowell
profiles.description: Matthew Lowell enlisted in the U.S. Army in April 2002 at age 17. After developing a specific moral and legal objection to the Iraq war, he went absent without leave in October 2003, returned after being promised a discharge, and left again in October 2004 when the discharge was cancelled and his unit received Iraq orders. Authorities arrested him at his grandmother’s home in September 2005 and returned him to his unit. He left again and entered Canada in November 2005. Amnesty International opposed his threatened 2008 deportation. The available sources do not state how long he remained under guard after the 2005 arrest or document jail or stockade confinement.
profiles.finding: Amnesty and wmtc deportation reports match Army 2002 and Canada 2005 history. Matthew Lowell Hostak obituary is a different person.

profiles.name: Priscilla Treska
profiles.description: Priscilla Treska was a Cleveland Montessori teacher, Catholic peace activist, and member of the Inter-Religious Task Force on Central America. During the 2005 School of the Americas Watch action at Fort Benning, she crossed onto the base in protest and deliberately refused bail, explaining that she would not participate in a bail system that punished people who could not pay. Treska remained in the Muscogee County Jail for 72 days. In late January 2006 she was convicted and released with a sentence of time served.
profiles.finding: Publici April 2008 SOAW roster provides context; no independently confirmed portrait located in initial search.

profiles.name: Corey Martin
profiles.description: Corey Martin was a U.S. Army intelligence sergeant at Fort Drum who applied for conscientious-objector discharge in December 2005. After an investigating officer recommended approval, the Army nevertheless ordered him to deploy to Afghanistan. The New York Civil Liberties Union obtained a temporary restraining order on March 10, 2006 and a further federal order on March 20 preventing deployment while the application and any judicial review remained pending. The Army ultimately granted him conscientious-objector status and an honorable discharge in May 2006. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: ACLU conscientious-objector victory matches. Air Force general, training sergeant and cyclist portraits not matched.

profiles.name: Brad McCall
profiles.description: Brad McCall enlisted in the U.S. Army on August 28, 2006 and was assigned to Colorado Springs after basic training. Accounts from soldiers returning from Iraq convinced him that he could not participate in the war, and he left without authorization after his efforts to pursue conscientious-objector status were brushed aside. Canadian authorities detained him when he presented a refugee claim at the border on September 19, 2007. He spent two nights in a Surrey jail before release and then lived in Vancouver while pursuing immigration relief.
profiles.finding: Georgia Straight, ZNetwork first-person account, Indybay interview and Fire This Time remain credible leads requiring original-image/caption/credit verification.
